text: This is the lesson that makes the whole project honest. Last lesson showed the quantum classifier's training mechanism works. This lesson actually measures it against a classical baseline on held-out real data, and reports exactly what happens, including a result that isn't flattering to the quantum side.

The classical baseline is deliberately simple and genuinely strong: predict Versicolor if petal length is at least 2.5 centimeters, otherwise Setosa — a threshold a human could write by hand. Six real Iris measurements, three Setosa, three Versicolor, held out and never used in training, provide the evaluation set.

Applying the threshold rule to all six samples gets every single one right, 6 out of 6, 100 percent. Running the quantum classifier from last lesson, with its one-step-trained parameters, on the same six samples: it correctly predicts all three Setosa samples as class zero, but also predicts class zero for all three Versicolor samples, which is wrong. That's 3 out of 6, 50 percent accuracy.

The honest explanation is specific, not vague. Last lesson's one gradient step used only the Setosa sample, so it only ever got pushed in the direction that helps classify Setosa, with no opportunity to learn Versicolor at all. This is a real, measured case of a model that hasn't actually been trained on the full dataset — not a statement about quantum circuits being incapable of solving this task. A genuine multi-sample, multi-iteration training run would very plausibly close most or all of this gap.

This closing lesson's write-up is next: the skill that matters most from this entire course, reporting what you actually found, accurately, in a way that neither oversells nor undersells a real result.
